title: DP II: Grid DP & Interval DP
relevance: High (Extremely common in OAs, especially path-finding grids and substring palindromes)
company_notes: Robot right/down max-coin / path grids → basic Grid DP (Amazon, Citadel). Merge adjacent slimes/stones by sum cost → Interval DP MCM. Longest palindromic subsequence / min insertions to palindrome (Google, Microsoft). Two players picking from array ends under optimal play → dp[L][R] minimax interval DP.

phases.goal: Confirm the candidate maps wording to Grid DP (2D path) versus Interval/Range DP (length-ordered subarrays/substrings).

must_hit.point: Grid DP navigates a 2D matrix (usually right/down) with state dp[r][c] depending on adjacent cells, often for min/max path sum or combinations.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names dp[r][c] fed by neighboring cells on a right/down (or similar) grid walk.

must_hit.point: Interval DP uses dp[L][R] on smaller intervals such as dp[L+1][R] or dp[L][k] + dp[k+1][R], filling shortest intervals before longer ones.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States dp[L][R] depends only on strictly smaller intervals and is ordered by length.

must_hit.point: Interval DP is the cue when you must merge adjacent elements, partition an array, or solve palindrome/game-theory questions on a substring.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists merge/partition/palindrome/end-pick game as the recognition triggers.

must_hit.point: OA wording like robot collecting coins on a board, merge-all min cost, longest palindromic subsequence, or two players picking ends maps to this family.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Matches at least two of those interview phrasings to Grid or Interval DP.

probes: What makes you pick Grid DP versus Interval DP on a new problem?
Which OA phrases scream robot-path grids, MCM merges, palindrome substrings, or end-pick games?

hints.1: Ask whether the state lives on a grid cell or on a contiguous [L,R] segment.
hints.2: Grid: right/down dp[r][c] from neighbors. Interval: merge/partition/palindrome/game, filled short→long.
hints.3: Say: Grid = dp[r][c] adjacent path/combos; Interval = dp[L][R] from smaller intervals by length; cues are merge, partition, palindrome, or end-pick games.

phases.goal: Get the candidate to name the right transition template: grid neighbors, length-ordered intervals, MCM split-k, game, or palindrome ends.

must_hit.point: Standard grid transitions read from (r-1, c) and (r, c-1) (with clean edge handling).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes or states those two parent cells as the usual grid recurrence.

must_hit.point: Interval fill loops length = 2...N, then L = 0...(N - length), with R = L + length - 1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that exact length-then-L ordering and R formula.

must_hit.point: Matrix Chain Multiplication style uses nested loops for L, for R, for k in L...R-1 to split the interval.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the triple loop and k as the split point.

must_hit.point: Zero-sum end-pick games set dp[L][R] = max(val[L] - dp[L+1][R], val[R] - dp[L][R-1]).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Quotes that max-of-two-ends recurrence.

must_hit.point: Palindromic interval DP matches ends: if S[L] == S[R] then dp[L][R] builds from dp[L+1][R-1] (plus the problem’s increment).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the equal-ends shortcut into the inner substring.

must_hit.point: For two agents moving simultaneously on a grid, enforce r1 + c1 = r2 + c2 = step to drop a state dimension.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions the shared step/diagonal equality as the dimension cut.

probes: Before coding, is this neighbor-grid DP, length-ordered interval DP, MCM split-k, end-pick game, or palindrome ends?
For two robots on one grid, how do you shrink the joint state?

hints.1: Classify path-on-grid vs interval-on-array/string, then pick the transition family.
hints.2: Grid uses (r-1,c)/(r,c-1); intervals use length→L→R; MCM adds k; games use the max ends formula; palindromes match S[L]/S[R].
hints.3: Say: neighbors (r-1,c),(r,c-1); length=2...N, R=L+length-1; for L,R,k in L...R-1; max(val[L]-dp[L+1][R], val[R]-dp[L][R-1]); equal ends → dp[L+1][R-1]; multi-agent → r1+c1=r2+c2=step.

phases.goal: Verify the candidate can write clean grid tables, previous-row rolling space, and the standard interval/MCM loop skeletons.

must_hit.point: Implement 2D Grid DP with dp[r][c] and explicit boundary checks when reading (r-1, c) and (r, c-1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sketches the 2D table and guards first row/column (or equivalent) cleanly.

must_hit.point: Space-optimize Grid DP from O(N*M) to O(M) by keeping only the previous row.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes rolling to a single prior-row array of width M.

must_hit.point: Code the interval skeleton: for length = 2...N, for L = 0...(N - length), set R = L + length - 1, then fill dp[L][R].
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes that nested length/L loop with the R assignment.

must_hit.point: For MCM-style merges, nest for k in L...R-1 inside the [L,R] cell (and use prefix sums when the merge cost needs range sums, as in Slimes).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows the k-split loop and mentions prefix sums when cost is a subarray sum.

probes: Write the grid recurrence with boundaries, then the length-ordered interval loops.
How do you roll grid space to the previous row, and where does the MCM k loop sit?

hints.1: Start from a Unique Paths / Min Path Sum table, then the length→L→R interval nest.
hints.2: Guard (r-1,c)/(r,c-1); roll to previous row O(M); intervals set R=L+length-1; MCM adds k in L...R-1.
hints.3: Say: dp[r][c] from (r-1,c)/(r,c-1) with edge guards; keep only prior row for O(M); length=2...N, L=0...(N-length), R=L+length-1; MCM for k in L...R-1 (+ prefix sums if needed).

phases.goal: State the file’s grid space reduction and the multi-agent state-dimension cut—without inventing asymptotics not in the source.

must_hit.point: Grid DP space can drop from O(N*M) to O(M) when only the previous row is needed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Quotes O(N*M) → O(M) via prior-row rolling.

must_hit.point: Simultaneous multi-agent grid DP uses r1 + c1 = r2 + c2 = step to cut one dimension from the joint state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains the shared step identity as the space/state reduction.

probes: How do you shrink a standard grid DP’s memory footprint?
How does the simultaneous two-agent constraint reduce state size?

hints.1: Separate full-table space from multi-agent state design.
hints.2: Previous-row rolling gives O(M); equal manhattan/step ties the two agents.
hints.3: Say: O(N*M)→O(M) keeping the previous row; enforce r1+c1=r2+c2=step to drop a dimension.

phases.goal: Catch wrong interval fill order, sloppy grid edges, forward-only survival DP, and boundary-blind MCM variants.

must_hit.point: Filling intervals in the wrong order (not shortest-to-longest) makes dp[L][R] read uncomputed smaller intervals.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names length-ordered processing as mandatory for correctness.

must_hit.point: Omitting clean (r-1, c) / (r, c-1) boundary checks corrupts first-row/first-column grid transitions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls out missing edge guards as the classic grid bug.

must_hit.point: Dungeon-style survival: a forward path state is insufficient to guarantee survival—need bottom-up thinking from the requirement side.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says forward DP alone cannot certify min HP / survival.

must_hit.point: Hard MCM variants like Burst Balloons make subproblems depend on the open boundaries, not only the interior split.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions that the interval’s bordering values enter the transition.

probes: What breaks if you fill dp[L][R] before shorter intervals, or skip grid edge guards?
Why is forward DP not enough for Dungeon Game, and what makes Burst Balloons harder than plain MCM?

hints.1: Check fill order, grid edges, and whether the ask needs a reverse/bottom-up survival view.
hints.2: Short→long intervals; guard first row/col; Dungeon needs bottom-up survival; Burst Balloons folds boundary balloons into the cost.
hints.3: List: wrong length order → stale/missing deps; missing (r-1,c)/(r,c-1) guards; forward state ≠ survival; Burst Balloons depends on interval boundaries.

tradeoffs.topic: Full O(N*M) grid table vs O(M) previous-row rolling
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Keep the full 2D table when you need all cells or multi-source combinations; if transitions only need the prior row, roll to O(M) space.

tradeoffs.topic: Grid DP (adjacent cells) vs Interval DP (length-ordered [L,R])
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use Grid DP for right/down (or jagged) path/combo boards; use Interval DP when the answer on a contiguous segment depends only on strictly smaller segments—merges, partitions, palindromes, end-pick games.

tradeoffs.topic: Endpoint-only interval transitions vs MCM split-at-k
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Palindrome/game styles often only touch dp[L+1][R], dp[L][R-1], or dp[L+1][R-1]; merge-all / stick-cut / triangulation needs an explicit k in L...R-1 (MCM).

tradeoffs.topic: Forward path DP vs bottom-up survival DP (Dungeon Game)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Ordinary min/max path sums work forward from the start; survival / min initial resource can require bottom-up formulation because forward state alone does not guarantee survival.

gotchas.trap: Computing dp[L][R] before all shorter intervals are done.
gotchas.correction: Process intervals ordered by length from shortest to longest (length = 2...N, then L, then R = L + length - 1).

gotchas.trap: Reading (r-1, c) or (r, c-1) without boundary handling on the first row/column.
gotchas.correction: Initialize edges carefully and only add a parent cell when it exists.

gotchas.trap: Trying to solve Dungeon Game with a normal forward min-path DP.
gotchas.correction: Forward state is insufficient to guarantee survival—formulate bottom-up from the survival requirement.

gotchas.trap: Tracking two simultaneous grid agents with a full 4D position state and no coupling.
gotchas.correction: Use r1 + c1 = r2 + c2 = step to cut a dimension from the state space.

gotchas.trap: Treating Burst Balloons like plain interior-only MCM.
gotchas.correction: In that MCM variation the subproblems depend on the boundary values around the interval, not only the split k.
